summary.text: Take the nonexceptional even value \(m=10\): the bound forces the prime \(q\le \lfloor 10/4\rfloor=2\) to equal \(2\), so \(10=p+q\) forces \(p=8\), which is not prime.

full_proof.text:
We disprove the even half of the conjecture by taking
\[
m=10.
\]
This is an admissible value for that half: it is even, it is greater than \(8\), and it is neither \(32\) nor \(152\).

Suppose, contrary to what we will prove, that the asserted representation exists for \(m=10\). Then there are primes \(p\) and \(q\) such that
\[
10=p+q,
\qquad
q\le \left\lfloor\frac{10}{4}\right\rfloor,
\]
and, in addition, for every prime divisor \(r\) of \(10+1=11\),
\[
\left(\frac{(q+1)/2}{r}\right)=1.
\]
Here the division in the bound is integer division, so
\[
\left\lfloor\frac{10}{4}\right\rfloor=2.
\]
Consequently \(q\le 2\). On the other hand, every prime natural number is at least \(2\). Since \(q\) is prime, we therefore have
\[
2\le q\le 2,
\]
and hence
\[
q=2.
\]
Substituting this into the required equation \(10=p+q\) gives
\[
10=p+2,
\]
so \(p=8\). But \(8\) is not prime, since \(8=2\cdot4\). This contradicts the requirement that \(p\) be prime.

Thus \(10\) has no representation satisfying even the primality, sum, and size conditions. In particular it cannot have a representation satisfying those conditions together with the additional Jacobi-symbol conditions; no evaluation of a Jacobi symbol is needed.

The conjecture asserts the even representation for every even \(m>8\) except \(32\) and \(152\). Since \(10\) meets its hypotheses but fails its conclusion, the even universal assertion is false. Therefore the conjunction of the odd and even assertions—the stated Sun refinement conjecture for A191004—is false.
